questions.q: What should a lesson plan state first?
options: The page numbers to copy
What children should be able to do by the end
The homework for the week
How long the teacher will talk

questions.q: Why use real objects like coins or leaves in a Class 2 lesson?
options: Young children learn best by seeing and touching
It saves time on the board
It keeps parents happy
It is only useful in art classes

questions.q: A lesson has 40 minutes. Which plan suits Class 3 best?
options: 40 minutes of the teacher reading aloud
Short explanation, group activity, then a quick check
Copying from the board the whole period
A test at the start, then free time

questions.q: Half the class finished the activity early. The rest are still working. What do you do?
options: Let them go and play outside
Tell them to sit silently and wait
Give the early group a harder extension task
Stop everyone and move on

questions.q: What does 'learning outcome' mean in a lesson plan?
options: The marks a child gets
The name of the chapter
The time at which the lesson ends
A skill the child can show after the lesson

options: Teach only to the middle level
Use one story with tasks at different levels
Let the strong readers teach the whole class
Give the weak readers colouring work instead

questions.q: A topic needs two periods, but you have one before the test. What is the best choice?
options: Cover the core idea well and plan a later recap
Rush through every page in one period
Skip the topic, it may not come

questions.q: What is a good way to get a noisy class's attention?
options: Shout louder than the class until it is quiet

Walk out of the room

questions.q: When should class rules be made clear to children?
options: Only after someone breaks them
At the end of the year
In the first days, with simple examples
Only in the parents' meeting

questions.q: A child keeps talking during your lesson. What do you do first?
options: Send them out of the class
Shout their name in front of everyone

questions.q: Why praise specific good behaviour, like 'Good, you put your books away'?
options: It is shorter than other praise
It stops all bad behaviour forever
It is needed only for toppers

questions.q: Two children fight over a pencil and one starts crying. What do you do?
options: Punish both of them at once
Give the pencil to the one crying
Calm both, hear each side, and help them solve it

questions.q: A child who is usually calm has been disruptive for a week. What should you do?
options: Punish them so it does not spread
Talk to them privately; something may be wrong
Move them to the last bench
Ignore it, it will stop by itself

questions.q: A child with ADHD can't sit still for long. How do you help them in class?
options: Make them sit on the last bench
Give extra homework to keep them busy
Send them home early each day
Give short tasks, movement breaks and clear steps

questions.q: A few students laugh whenever one shy child answers. What do you do?
options: Ignore it, children always tease
Stop it firmly, set a respect rule, and support the child
Stop asking the shy child any questions in class
Laugh along to keep the mood light

questions.q: Physical punishment of children in Indian schools is:
options: Allowed for serious mistakes
Allowed if parents agree
Banned under the RTE Act
Left to the teacher to decide

questions.q: A child falls and cuts a knee in the playground. What do you do first?
options: Tell them to wash it at home
Wait and ignore it once they stop crying
Send them home alone
Clean it, apply a plaster from the first-aid kit, inform the office

questions.q: At home time, a stranger says they have come to pick up a Class 1 child. What do you do?
options: Don't hand over; check with the parent and office
Let the child go if the person knows the name
Let the child decide
Send the child, as it is getting late

questions.q: A child tells you an adult at home hurts them and asks you to keep it secret. What do you do?
options: Promise to keep it a secret
Listen calmly, don't promise secrecy, report to the head
Call the adult and ask them about it

questions.q: A child often comes to school hungry and sleepy. What is a good first step?
options: Scold them for sleeping in class
Talk gently to them and tell the school counsellor
Tell the class about it
Ignore it, it is a home matter

questions.q: When tutoring a child at their home, what is good practice?
options: Lock the door to stop noise
Keep the child's parents away
Meet in a closed room for focus
Sit in an open room where adults can see

questions.q: A child in your class has a peanut allergy, and children share lunch. What do you do?
options: Let them share, small bits are fine
Make the child eat alone outside
Tell the parents to keep the child at home

questions.q: A Class 1 child can't read the word 'cat'. What helps most?
options: Sound out c-a-t together, then blend it
Ask them to copy it 20 times
Tell them the word and move on
Give a harder word to challenge them

questions.q: Why read stories aloud to young children every day?
options: It builds vocabulary and a love for reading
It only keeps them quiet
It replaces writing practice
It is only for weak readers

questions.q: A child reads a passage well but can't answer any question about it. What skill needs work?
options: Handwriting
Spelling
Speed of reading
Understanding (comprehension)

questions.q: A child speaks a different language at home and is new to English. How do you help them?
options: Ban the home language completely in class
Use pictures, gestures and some home-language words
Give English-only tests first
Seat them alone to focus

questions.q: Which activity best improves spoken English in Class 4?
options: Short role plays in pairs
Copying sentences from the board
Silent reading only
Learning grammar rules by heart

questions.q: A Class 3 child often writes 'b' for 'd' and reads slowly, despite trying hard. What do you do?
options: Tell the parents the child is lazy and careless
Make them repeat the year
Note it, give extra support and suggest a specialist check

questions.q: What is the best way to correct many errors in a child's essay?
options: Mark every mistake in red
Pick two or three key errors and show the fix
Rewrite the essay for them
Give zero marks so they try harder next time

questions.q: What is the best way to start teaching addition to Class 1?
options: With two-digit sums on the board
By memorising answers
With word problems only
With counters, beads or fingers

questions.q: A child says 7 + 5 = 11. What is a good response?
options: Say 'wrong' and move on
Tell them it is 12 and continue
Ask them to count it again with counters
Mark it wrong in red pen

questions.q: Which tool best helps children understand tens and ones?
options: Bundles of 10 sticks and loose sticks
A ruler
A number chart up to 10
A protractor

questions.q: A child writes 25 + 17 = 312. What is the likely mistake?
options: Subtracting instead of adding
Not knowing that 5 + 7 = 12
Not carrying over the ten
Reading 17 as 71

questions.q: How do you best explain 1/2 and 1/4 to Class 3?
options: Fold or cut a roti or paper into equal parts
Write the definitions on the board
Teach the LCM method first
Use only number lines

questions.q: Many children get a word problem wrong but can do the sum itself. What do you do?
options: Give only plain sums from now on, no word problems
Give the answers to copy
Practise reading the problem and picking the operation
Move on to the next chapter

questions.q: A child says 0.25 is bigger than 0.5 because 25 is more than 5. How do you correct this?
options: Compare using place value or a 100-square grid
Tell them to just remember it
Say longer decimals are always smaller
Skip decimals for now

questions.q: In a mixed tuition group, one child is far ahead in maths and gets bored. What do you do?
options: Give challenge problems while others practise basics
Ask them to wait quietly
Make them teach every lesson to the others
Send them home early

questions.q: What is the main use of a short quiz at the end of a lesson?
options: To fill the period
To find and punish the noisy children
To see who understood and who needs help
To give ranks

questions.q: How should you share a child's weak result with parents?
options: In front of other parents
By saying the child is weak
Privately, with examples and a plan to help
Only through the report card

questions.q: What does 'continuous assessment' mean?
options: One big exam at year end
Weekly ranks pasted on the classroom wall
Grading only homework neatness
Checking learning often, through class work and tasks

questions.q: A parent is upset about low marks and blames you. What do you do?
options: Listen calmly, show the work, and agree on next steps
Argue that the child is lazy
Raise the marks to please them
Tell them to complain to the principal

questions.q: How does a rubric help children in a speaking task?
options: It makes their marks higher
It saves paper
They know what good work looks like
It replaces feedback

questions.q: A parent asks you to give their child extra marks because of a family problem. What do you do?
options: Add the marks quietly
Refuse kindly; offer extra support or a retest if rules allow
Agree, and tell other parents about it
Refuse and end the meeting

questions.q: Most of the class got the same test question wrong. What is the best conclusion?
options: The class is weak
Cut marks for everyone
Never use that question again in any test
Reteach the idea and check if the question was clear

task.title: Write a progress note to a parent
task.brief: You are Aditi's class teacher. Read your notes and her father's message below. Take about 15 minutes and write a reply to the father (about 150–200 words). A good reply is warm and honest, starts with strengths, explains the areas to work on in simple words, gives 2–3 practical things the family can do even with little time, says what you will do in class, and invites a short meeting. Do not label the child as weak.
task.material:
Child: Aditi (Class 3), notes from the last 6 weeks
- Reading: reads Class 2 level stories fluently; slows down and guesses on new long words.
- Comprehension: answers 'what happened' questions well; struggles with 'why' questions.
- Maths: strong in addition and subtraction with carrying; unsure of multiplication tables beyond 5.
- Class work: neat, finishes on time. Homework missing 4 times in the last 2 weeks.
- Behaviour: helpful, kind to classmates; has become quiet in class this month.
- Test: 14/25 in English, 21/25 in Maths.

Message from her father on the school app:
"Aditi got only 14 in English. Is she weak? Should we put her in extra tuition? We are both working and can't sit with her daily.
key_points: Warm greeting and thanks for reaching out
Starts with real strengths: maths, neat work, kindness
Explains English needs: new long words and 'why' questions, in simple words
Does not call the child weak; says tuition is not the only answer
2–3 practical home tips that fit busy parents (10 minutes of reading, asking 'why' about a story, homework routine)
Mentions missing homework and that she has become quiet, gently, and asks if anything has changed
Says what the teacher will do in class and invites a short meeting

rubric.label: Tone
rubric.guide: 0 = cold, blaming or labels the child, 3 = polite but flat, 5 = warm, respectful and encouraging

rubric.label: Accurate picture
rubric.guide: 0 = ignores or misreads the notes, 3 = covers some points, 5 = strengths and needs match the notes, including homework and quietness

rubric.label: Practical advice
rubric.guide: 0 = no advice, 3 = general advice, 5 = 2–3 specific tips a busy family can follow, plus the teacher's own plan

rubric.label: Clarity
rubric.guide: 0 = confusing or too long, 3 = understandable, 5 = simple words, well organised, right length
